svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. The two costs that every extension carries
svg.desc: One benefit and two costs. The benefit is whatever protection the extension provides. The first cost is entropy: research fingerprinted between nine and twenty-three percent of evaluated extensions, and among 854 real users many carried a distinctive set. The second cost is trust: a content blocker needs to read and alter every page, and three documented incidents show what happens when that trust is misplaced.
svg.text: The paradox is usually stated and rarely quantified. Here are the numbers behind it.

svg.text: Three times that trust was misplaced

g.text: A site reputation extension that was
found to be selling detailed browsing
histories. Pulled from the stores.
Sold what it was trusted to protect.
A styling extension, sold to an analytics
firm, then quietly updated to report
every site its users visited.
The code was fine when you installed it.
Researchers found a coordinated set of
extensions injecting ads and exfiltrating
data. Around 500 were removed.
Store presence is not review.

svg.text: The rule that falls out of this
A small number of widely used extensions from maintainers with a long record. Popularity matters here in a way it usually does not, because a common extension hides
you in a larger group and gets far more scrutiny. Two of the three cases above began as a change of ownership, so check who maintains a tool now, not who wrote it.
